item.title: If Your Therapist Gets Sick, Do You Want to Know?
item.description:
Boundaries

If Your Therapist Gets Sick, Do You Want to Know?

When the therapist gets a serious health diagnosis, what should they disclose?

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists model good boundaries, but illness puts self-disclosure of highly private information on the table.
  • Clients talk about themselves; therapists don't, on the whole. That may change with illness.
  • Although confidentiality is a cornerstone of psychotherapy, it doesn't apply to the therapist.
  • A serious health diagnosis is one of those terrible therapeutic opportunities.

Co-authored by Martha Sweezy and Roberta Omin

Imagine you are a therapy client arriving for a session. You watch your therapist walk across the room with a limp. He seems to be in pain; he looks tired and preoccupied. Part of you feels concerned and wants to ask if he’s okay. Another part admonishes internally, “It’s none of your business! That’s how it goes in therapy.”

Now imagine being the therapist. Your limp is a big tell. You’re not sleeping well, you feel exhausted, and it's no wonder – you just got a troubling diagnosis. You are scared, and when you woke up this morning, you felt overwhelmed. You are aware of being deeply vulnerable. No part of you wants to share this information with clients. As you sit down, you hear some inner reassurance, “Don’t worry. We don’t have to talk about it.”

A Therapeutic Dilemma

Internal Family Systems therapy (IFS) maintains that the mind — the arena of subjective experience — is peopled with parts, or subjectively experienced individuals of all ages who live in an inner community but, just like people, are motivated by different perspectives and concerns. In IFS therapy, we get curious and question the parts who show up. Each one has a backstory. Take Sabra, the client in this example.

Her parts are in an uproar:

  • What if this is serious? What will I do if he’s really sick? And I can’t even ask him.
  • I’ve been noticing little changes, but this is clearer today.
  • Look, he’ll tell you if he thinks it’s important. Trust him!
  • Yeah right! Whenever anyone gets sick, I’m the last one to know. Secrets are always kept from me.
  • Why does this keep happening to me? As usual, I’m always treated like the baby.
  • Let’s get a new therapist.
  • If we can’t trust Daniel to be honest, who can we trust?
  • Why should we trust anyone?

And so on. Meanwhile, the therapist, Daniel, is also hearing from many parts:

  • Sabra is noticing my walk. I thought I could keep it hidden. What do I do now if she asks me about it?
  • I can’t bear to talk about what is really happening to me right now. I’m so vulnerable. I’m terrified and overwhelmed.
  • You buck up and do your job.
  • And besides, this is strictly private. You don’t owe your clients explanations about your health, and you have to maintain professional boundaries.
  • Right, it’s not her job to take care of me.
  • Be realistic! This isn’t going to go away. We don’t even know if you’ll be able to go on working. Everyone’s going to know at some point.
  • Oh, so you’re ready to talk about this?
  • Look, just take care of yourself like you always do. You’ll find a way to handle this.

While going through the ritual beginning of a therapy session, Sabra and Daniel are experiencing parallel inner hubbubs. Over the next few weeks, as they don’t talk about it and he remains visibly symptomatic, the hubbubs grow louder. The elephant is in the room. How does this affect therapy? Everything changes. Rather than exploring, they both inhibit, each for their own reason. Without conscious intention, they call their protective parts to the battlements and send their vulnerable parts to the castle depths.

Who Are These Vulnerable Parts?

Sabra’s vulnerable parts were infantilized, uncherished, unsafe, and over-and-under-protected from the behaviors of authority figures who did one thing and said another.

Daniel’s vulnerable parts don’t want to be exposed. They feel inadequate and shamed, particularly compared to smarter, more valued people at home and in school.

Do Therapists Need Privacy? Do Clients Need to Know?

Yes.

If the therapist wants privacy but believes the client needs to know, whose needs come first?

When it gets complicated, the therapist needs a therapist — and supervision — to sort it out. Though painful, this process is their opportunity to engage in what IFS calls a U-turn — a pivot to their inner world, their vulnerable parts, and seminal experiences of early shaming. The best guide through the Minotaur’s maze is the one who has already gone through it — if they’ve paid kind attention to the experience their parts had in the maze.

Sorting the Personal and Professional

Therapists are taught to be cautious about sharing personal information with clients for good reason. Therapists also prefer to keep what is personal out of their professional realm. It’s the job of therapists to model good boundaries. We can’t mean “yes” or “no” without clear boundaries. A genuine “yes” and a genuine “no” are essential relational tools. At the same time, life requires flexibility. Generalized rules can’t cover every contingency.

When an illness or accident disrupts our personal lives, it will likely affect our professional lives. Since therapy is a “relationship” profession, the illness of the therapist puts self-disclosure on the table, sometimes of necessity (due to medical treatment, absence, abrupt cancellations, or forced retirement), and sometimes because the illness is noticeable.

How we handle that disclosure can have a profound impact on the therapeutic relationship, especially when it touches on a client’s traumatic past or current problem. Sabra’s mother, for example, died of cancer when she was 12 years old. Beyond informing the client, disclosure is often a therapeutic opportunity, a potential for a corrective relational experience, and a chance to help the client with their fear of loss and abandonment, inhibited grief, and penchant for self-sacrifice.

Do the Right Thing

In IFS, we build relationships on multiple levels at once, both inside and out. Therapy is a co-creation, carefully nourished and tended by relational attunement. The goal of IFS therapy is to come to parts from the zoomed-out perspective of the Self, the “I” in all of us that’s characterized by compassion, courage, curiosity, and love, among many other fine qualities. When therapist and client can both access these resources, they find their way to doing the right thing.

item.title: The Tricky Business of Calculating Risks and Rewards
item.description:
Self-Help

The Tricky Business of Calculating Risks and Rewards

Does a social safety net reduce risk tolerance?

Posted September 15, 2026

Psychologists define risk tolerance as a relatively stable characteristic, reflecting core personality traits. Risk tolerance is, nonetheless, subject to change, as individuals age and respond to recent events, set in the context of their past and present life circumstances, their behavioral biases, and their assessment of risk and reward. And risk tolerance is domain-specific. The same person can have a high tolerance for risk in investments, while prioritizing safety when arranging a blind date.

In Worth the Risk: The Seven Myths That Keep Us from Taking the Chances We Need To Take, Allison Schrager (a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute and author of An Economist Walks Into A Brothel: And Other Unexpected Places To Understand Risk) argues that Americans have become increasingly risk-averse, a development that portends diminished returns and higher costs for them and the United States. The world, she declares, “has never been safer, and there has never been a better time to take risks.”

Focused mostly, but not exclusively, on financial and investment decisions, Schrager’s book is adorned with thumbnail sketches of risk-takers, including Harland Sanders, the founder of Kentucky Fried Chicken, and the Wallenda family of tightrope walkers.

An informative and engaging examination of an important topic, Worth the Risk is provocative, but not always persuasive.

Schrager acknowledges daunting challenges to her thesis. “Without a common definition of safety,” she writes, “it is hard to know what should be considered risky behavior. And because risk is a nebulous concept, many of us define it based on emotion, not rational probability.”

Schrager speculates that the federal government reforms of the 1960s and ‘70s — Medicare, Medicaid, Food Stamps, school lunch programs, disaster relief, consumer and environmental protection laws — convinced many Americans that risk “was something to be reduced or eliminated.” In the ensuing decades, she indicates, the word risk has taken on “negative connotations.”

One might theorize, just as credibly, however, that the social safety net provides a financial foundation that encourages risk-taking.

Moreover, Schrager assesses alternative explanations of the decline in risk tolerance in passing or not at all. Americans over 65, who are less willing to take risks, regardless of macroeconomic developments in the United States, for example, now comprise almost 20% of our nation’s population, up from 10% in 1970. More than three-quarters of Americans, including a high proportion of 40-somethings, have grown more financially cautious in response to the Great Recession, the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation, rising health care costs, and the potential impact of A.I. on jobs. The growing unwillingness of Americans to start small businesses reflects a grim reality: 9 out of every 10 of them fail.

Schrager endorses claims that the risk aversion of adolescents that has manifested itself in declines in substance abuse, unprotected sex, crime, and dangerous automobile driving is due to “helicopter parenting” and social media use, which has resulted in less unstructured time with friends and acquaintances. She cites a study by cultural psychologist Yulia Chentsova-Dutton, which asserts that less exposure to risk at this age is changing brain development in ways that make it more difficult to deal with setbacks in adulthood.

And Schrager notes a recent phenomenon that doesn’t fit the thesis of rampant risk aversion: the decision of many Gen Z Americans to bet lots of money on sports contests and crypto stocks.

In the end, Worth the Risk is mostly hortatory. Shrager knows that a third of Americans do not have sufficient savings to sustain them for a month, but doesn’t think “anyone can argue that people with less means need to take fewer risks.” She seconds the proposal of psychologist Abigail Baird that the best time to train your brain to take risks “is when it’s still forming,” even though things may still feel unstable. Schrager exhorts her readers to “find the courage to change jobs more frequently.” She insists “you never age out of risk-taking.”

“Maintain a healthy perspective,” Schrager concludes. “The downside to risk-taking is probably not as bad as you think, because the world has never been safer. Odds are you will bounce back even if a risk goes badly. We have more options and second chances than any other time in history.”

What, then, should one make of Schrager’s paean to risk-takers and risk-taking? Perhaps Robert Oppenheimer had it right: “The optimist thinks that this is the best of all possible worlds,” he wrote, “and the pessimist knows it.”

item.title: Why Do I Keep Replaying Conversations in My Head?
item.description:
Anxiety

Why Do I Keep Replaying Conversations in My Head?

What we are trying to figure out after the conversation is already over.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Fear of rejection can make small details feel much more meaningful than they are.
  • You can spend hours replaying a conversation without getting any closer to knowing what someone thought.
  • Reassurance may bring temporary relief, but repeatedly seeking it can keep the anxiety going.
  • Feeling embarrassed afterward does not necessarily mean you did something wrong.

You had dinner with your girlfriends. It was a fun night. You laughed a lot, as usual, and even put a date on your calendars for the next night out. Later that night, as you wash your face before bed, something you said at dinner comes back to you. You noticed it at the time but didn’t think much of it, and the uneasy feeling quickly passed. Now you’re replaying the interaction and wondering whether you came across as rude. Did you interrupt someone? You know you tend to do that. Was the joke you told actually funny? What was that look on one friend’s face? Was she irritated that you asked about her marriage?

Source: Photo by Alexandra Gorn on Unsplash

This is where an ordinary interaction can take on outsized importance. Everything someone does starts to feel like a judgment, criticism, or a sign they're upset with you. You remember one friend eyeing the server for the check while you were in the middle of a story, and you wonder if she was bored. Soon, you’re wondering whether you bored the whole table and whether they texted each other afterward to talk about you. You may even start imagining them figuring out how to avoid the next dinner or planning when they can get together without you.

In my private practice as a psychotherapist, I see this often. Rather than simply calling it “overthinking” and focusing only on how to stop, I am interested in what someone is trying to accomplish by replaying the interaction. The reality is, you probably remember what happened. What you don’t know, and what you’re trying to figure out, is what the other person thought of you.

What Are You Really Trying to Find Out?

When you’re trying to work out what someone thinks of you, almost anything can become a clue. Your friend asking for the check might mean she was offended and couldn’t wait to leave. It might also mean she was tired after a long week, didn’t like driving at night, or had to get up early. Once you’re embarrassed or worried, those explanations don’t tend to get equal consideration.

Confirmation bias can take over from there. If you’re afraid that you interrupt too much, you remember every time you started speaking before someone had finished. You may even question whether you listened to the rest of your friend’s story. If you worry that people find you annoying, someone checking her phone suddenly seems important. The laughter, the parts of the conversation that flowed easily, and the plans for another dinner begin to count for less. None of that proves that nobody was ever irritated, but anxiety tends to treat anything that might signal rejection as evidence and everything else as inconclusive.

Wanting to know whether your friend was annoyed is usually not just about her mood at dinner. Another question often lies underneath: What would it mean about me if she was? “I said something awkward” becomes “I am awkward.” “She seemed annoyed” becomes “People find me annoying.” The replay is no longer about one conversation. It gets mixed up with older fears and, in some cases, lived experiences that led to core beliefs that you are unlovable, unworthy, too much, or not someone other people will want to keep around.

Rumination can be a way of trying to protect yourself from having those fears confirmed and feeling the pain you may have felt in the past. If you can identify the exact moment when you “messed up,” maybe you can correct it, avoid doing it again, and keep anyone from rejecting you. You try to become beyond reproach, as if getting every interaction right could spare you from criticism, misunderstanding, or hurt. Since nobody can do that, you end up watching yourself and everyone around you even more closely. By then, a lot more is riding on the dinner than anything that actually happened at the table.

Source: Photo by Toa Heftiba on Unsplash

The Conversation You Wish You Had

I suspect most of us have had this experience. Several hours, or even days, after a conversation, we know exactly what we should have said or done differently. In the revised version, you are more confident, less awkward, and know exactly when to stop talking. It is remarkable what you can pull off once the other person is no longer in the room, you have had three hours to prepare, and hindsight is doing some of the work for you.

Of course, looking back can be useful. Heck, that is often part of what you get to do in therapy. It can help you notice patterns or plan how to respond if something similar happens again. Sometimes you realize you were insensitive or defensive, or that you missed what someone was trying to tell you. If thinking about an interaction leads to insight, an apology, or a decision to do something differently next time, it has served a purpose.

Then again, embarrassment is not always a sign that you did anything wrong. You may have rambled, lost your train of thought, made a joke that didn’t land, or heard yourself say something and immediately wished you had worded it differently. It may bother you afterward, but that does not necessarily mean you hurt someone or need to go back and “fix” the conversation.

When Reassurance Turns Into Another Round

When you can’t decide whether you did something wrong, you may ask someone you trust what they think. Their answer may quell your anxiety at first. If you have what I call a sticky brain, however, it soon finds a detail you forgot to mention or a reason their reassurance may not count. Before long, you’re asking the same question again just in a slightly different way.

You might recount what happened at dinner and ask whether you sounded rude. When they say they don’t think so, you feel better for a moment. Then you remember that they didn’t hear exactly how you made a particular comment, so you act it out, trying to recreate your inflection and body language. When they still aren’t convinced that you were rude or that your friends were offended and planning to exclude you, you push back harder. They didn’t see the way the others looked at one another while you were talking. They weren’t there to catch the small shifts in their expressions.

There is nothing wrong with asking someone you trust for perspective. Again, that’s often what happens inside the therapy room. It becomes a problem when every answer leads to another worry. At that point, you’re no longer asking what the person thinks. You’re hoping they can give you certainty that what you fear is not true: a certainty that no one can give.

Reassurance can feel satisfying in the moment, which is why you return to it. It may also teach your brain that you need someone else to settle the question each time it comes up. Since its effects are short-lasting, it can leave both people frustrated. You ultimately don’t feel sure, and the person trying to help has run out of ways to answer you.

What If You Did Get It Wrong?

Relationships leave room for people to be awkward, misunderstand one another, and have moments they do not handle perfectly. You can care about how you affect people and make repairs when needed without treating every misstep as proof something is inherently wrong with you. The bigger issue is believing you have to get every interaction right to remain worthy of love and connection.

item.title: Using Neuroscience to Understand and Teach Rhythmic Meters
item.description:
Neuroscience

Using Neuroscience to Understand and Teach Rhythmic Meters

One person's enduring engagement with musical pedagogy Down Under.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Meter is typically thought of as the repeating pattern of strong and weak beats in a piece of music.
  • In a newer view of meter, it’s a relationship of pulses we experience, felt in time in our brains and bodies.
  • An awareness of these ideas may lead to methods that improve how meter is taught.

Several months ago, an email from Australia arrived in my inbox—it’s not every day I receive a letter from Down Under—and this is how our across-the-globe conversation got started. Andrea Calilhanna, a doctoral candidate in music education, introduced herself. She explained that she had read my book, Music Between Your Ears, and invited me to be a guest on her “Let’s Talk” music podcast.1 As we planned and recorded the podcast, I learned that Andrea has a keen interest in rhythm, especially musical meter. After the interview, I returned the favor by asking if I could interview her for my blog about her background and her research. This post is the result.

A Fascination With Meter

Music has played a central role in Andrea Calilhanna's life for many years. She studied piano, saxophone, and music theory at the Queensland Conservatorium, earning a diploma in piano performance; she then completed a teacher training program. While raising her family, she performed with various chamber ensembles, rock bands, and jazz groups. She has also taught piano for over 40 years. As a teacher, she noticed that many students struggle with timing and expression, so she began to search for better ways to teach this essential skill.

As her children grew up, she returned to school to earn a master's degree in music at the University of Sydney. Attending lectures on meter by Professor Richard Cohn, visiting from Yale University, she found the answer to her search. Cohn’s meter classes led Andrea to rethink how she taught meter. She began applying his theories with school-age students, helping them recognize and perform meter accurately. The positive results marked a turning point for her teaching and research. Her master’s thesis examined how students learn meter as a relationship among pulses, rather than simply as a notation system of time signatures and written music.2

Andrea’s desire to teach meter more effectively gradually led her to an important realization: “I needed to know about neuroscience.” This work led her to develop Ski-Hill Graph Pedagogy Meter Fundamentals, which is the focus of her current doctoral-candidate research at the University of Adelaide.3

What Is Meter?

Meter classically refers to the recurring patterns of strong and weak pulses within a piece of music. Most musical meters are built upon multiples of 2 (duple meter) or 3 (triple meter) beats per measure. The foundational meter of a march, for example, is 2:1 (2 beats per measure) in a strong-weak pattern; for a waltz, it’s 3:1 (3 beats per measure) in a strong-weak-weak pattern.

Typically, each beat lasts the same amount of time, and the strong beat is emphasized by being played louder. Expression, however, is not created by volume alone. Musicians can also shape meter by slightly lengthening strong pulses and shortening weak pulses. These subtle timing shifts enhance music’s expressive interest.

Mapping Meter

Cohn’s lectures introduced Andrea to the concept that meter is something we experience as pulses rather than simply count as beats. He also demonstrated how these pulses can be displayed in a pyramid-shaped diagram called a ski-hill graph. This visual map displays the various repeating pulse patterns contained in a piece of music.

Ski-hill graphs help students better understand and appreciate meter
Source: Photo from Clap, Tap and Map: Meter Fundamentals through Ski-hill Graph Pedagogy by Andrea Calilhanna (2025) ISBN: 979-8266573109. Used here with the author’s permission.

Since musical meters are built upon multiples of 2 or 3 beats per measure, using a ski-hill graph (see picture) helps students identify these repeating patterns as fractions, making it easier to understand and appreciate rhythmic structures for timing and expression within a piece of music. Experiencing meters as pulses that are felt in time is helpful because not all beats are heard: In syncopation, for example, a rest falls on the beat while the note is played off the beat.

Cohn’s contemporary definition of meter and ski-hill graph visualization helps students keep meters’ temporal pulses in mind, acknowledge each pulse division, and develop meter listening skills. In addition, whereas conventional meter theory only focuses on the foundational pulse, ski-hill graphs enable students to see and experience multiple rhythmic patterns. As a result, their timing and understanding of rhythm improve.

Rhythm and Movement Are Inseparable

Functional imaging studies show that the components of rhythm, including meter, are processed by both the brain’s hearing (auditory) and movement (motor) systems. Even when people stay still and listen to music, the motor system is active as it helps the brain recognize rhythm as well as produce rhythmic movements.4

How does this happen? Does the hearing system learn over time to communicate rhythmic patterns to the movement system, or are the two systems naturally linked from birth and pulse directly with the music’s rhythm?

Neural Resonance Theory to Explain Rhythm

Calilhanna favors the latter option and is a fan of Neural Resonance Theory (NRT). According to NRT, “pulse and meter arise as a result of neural oscillations resonating to rhythmic stimulation.”5 In other words, groups of brain cells naturally synchronize their activity with the rhythm of the music, initiating meter. For example, a song played at 180 beats per minute produces a primary beat at 3 hertz (Hz)—i.e., three beats per second. NRT holds that certain brain cells fire at that same frequency. And, because most music contains several rhythmic layers, different groups of brain cells may synchronize with different pulse rates simultaneously.6

Other rhythmic bursts of brain activity enable the hearing and movement systems to communicate with one another. This allows us to perceive rhythm as well as move in time with it.7 NRT asserts that this communication occurs through neural activity at frequencies higher than the rhythms pulsing within a piece of music.8

Since these brain cell firing patterns are biologically based, they occur synchronously in everyone listening to the same piece of music. For NRT, this shared brain activity explains entrainment, the tendency of people to move together naturally when listening to the same song.

The Musical Human

Curious about how she communicates these ideas in a nontechnical manner, I asked Andrea how she explains these complex scientific concepts to people without a background in neuroscience. How, for example, does she describe them to the person sitting next to her on a bus listening to music? “I point out to them that, even without knowing what it is, they’re engaging with meter when they bob their head or tap their feet. I also tell them, 'You’re musical because you’re human.'"

item.title: Safety-Seeking and Chronic Illness
item.description:
Chronic Illness

Safety-Seeking and Chronic Illness

To live with chronic illness is to have extended experiences of not feeling safe.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic illness can cause us to highly value safety.
  • Safety-seeking behaviors can be both adaptive and limiting.
  • Expanding life to include exploration as well as safety is a highly individual process.
Source: Katie Willard-Virant

To live with chronic illness is to have frequent and extended experiences of not feeling safe. Managing this felt lack of safety necessitates the expenditure of a significant amount of psychic energy. We become highly attuned to our bodies, monitoring our health closely. We associate certain activities with symptom improvement (e.g., heating pad, rest) and others with symptom exacerbation (e.g., eating certain foods, disrupted sleep). We learn to “read” our bodies in order to make decisions about what we need to do — and avoid — to stay as healthy as possible.

In the treatment of anxiety disorders, there is a recognition that anxiety causes people to act in ways that manage their distress. For example, someone who is afraid of flying may avoid airline travel. Someone afraid of the dark may sleep with a light on. Clinicians call these behavior modifications “safety-seeking behaviors” (Thwaites & Freeston, 2005). Safety-seeking behaviors are highly adaptive: We identify what we fear, and we change our behavior as a means of keeping anxiety at bay.

This is great, right? We orient our behavior to keep us as close to homeostasis as possible. However, we humans are not just wired to seek safety; we also are wired to grow and explore. Paradoxically, we are meant not only to adapt to our environment, but also to act upon it. This raises an important question: When does safety-seeking give us a secure launch pad from which to explore, and when does it impede exploration?

Safety is an important need for all people. Because illness continually threatens safety, safety-seeking can be especially prominent in people living with chronic illness. We are meticulous about following our medical regimen. We carefully attend to diet, exercise, and rest. We plan our days cautiously to avoid symptom exacerbation. These are positive coping behaviors. Why is it, then, that we still feel unfulfilled, anxious, and depressed? Certainly, there is the grief of the unchangeable limitations imposed by illness. But might there also be the grief of self-imposed limiting beliefs and behaviors?

The spoon theory is a terrific way of explaining the difficulty of life with chronic illness. The premise is that chronically ill people have a limited number of “spoons” (energy) that get used up very quickly. The battery metaphor is another apt description: People who live with illness have an energy battery that is never full and depletes quickly. Consequently, spoons/charge must be fiercely protected. People living with illness continually have to make judicious choices about how to expend their energy. “No” becomes a familiar stance: “I cannot take on that extra project at work; I cannot wash my hair tonight; I cannot attend that party.” I want to emphasize how important this “no” stance is to maintaining optimal health.

However, “no” can become so embedded that it takes on an automatic quality. We say “no” to everything because we believe our “no” is what keeps us safe. We become fearful of expending energy, and we hoard our limited spoons in case we need them later. We are investing so much energy into keeping ourselves safe that we have little left over for experiencing new things, for taking chances, for growing.

Adaptive coping or anxious safety-seeking?

You may be asking: How the heck can I tell the difference between saving spoons and hoarding spoons, between protecting my health and wrapping my body in bubble wrap? It’s an ever-shifting calculus that only you can evaluate. I invite you to sit with the following questions:

Am I fulfilled? You might think, “Well, no, I’m not fulfilled because I live with this illness.” Fair enough. But go deeper. Ask yourself what you would do if you did not live with illness. Would you travel? Pursue a particular work path? Be more social? What would you like your life to be like if the limits of your illness were taken away?

Are there ways of moving closer to the fulfillment I seek? Perhaps you would be an astronaut if your illness didn’t make that impossible. What would it feel like to watch films and read books about space? To visit your local Science Center? To follow astronauts on social media?

Do my baseline days look different from my flare days? Most of us know that on flare days we’re treading water at best. When you are not flaring, are you swimming at all — even a little dogpaddle? Our baseline days should not exhaust us, but arguably should feel different from flare days. What would it look like to spend some spoons on baseline days in ways that expand fulfillment?

Am I saying “no” to experiences because I am too ill or because I am afraid of becoming too ill? Protection instincts tend to run high in people living with illness. Is our fear of flaring so great that it causes us to automatically say no, without considering whether or not we actually have the spoons to say yes?

No shame, no blame

I’m aware that many people with chronic illness berate themselves (and are berated) for the ways they live cautiously in the service of managing their illness. This post is not meant to add distress. You, and only you, have the capacity to determine how you need to protect and optimize your health. I simply invite you to consider whether and how there may be room in your life to move (safely) beyond safety-seeking.
